info.title: SoftTrack
info.description: An open-source, self-hostable issue tracker inspired by Linear.

get.description:
What the sign-in and sign-up pages need before anyone has a token.

Public by necessity: the register page has to know whether to show a form
or an "ask an admin for a link" notice, and it asks before authenticating.
It reveals only that this instance is invite-only, whether it has a landing
page, whether it is the demo, and which sign-in providers are set up -- all
four of which the signed-out pages say out loud anyway. Note the last one
is provider *names*, never their client ids: the id is public in an
authorization URL, but it does not have to be published to anyone who can
reach the host.

post.description:
Email a single-use link for choosing a new password.

Always 204, whether or not the address has an account, so the answer
cannot be used to find out which addresses do. The mail goes out after
the response for the same reason: an SMTP round trip is slow enough to
time.

Set a new password with the token from a reset link.

The link works once. Every session the account had is signed out, and
the next step is signing in with the new password.
Change the password, and return a token so this tab stays signed in.

get.description: Your personal API tokens, without their secrets.

schema.title: Response List Api Tokens Auth Me Tokens Get

post.description:
Make a token for a script: `Authorization: Bearer softtrack_…`.

The response is the only time the secret is shown. It acts as you, with
your permissions, until it expires or is revoked. Tokens can only be
managed from a signed-in session, never with another token.

delete.description: Revoke a token. It stops working on the very next request.

schema.title: Response My Invites Auth Me Invites Get

post.description:
Redeem a finished sign-in for a session.

Deliberately unauthenticated and deliberately a POST: the ticket and the
handshake together are the credential, and neither belongs in a URL.

Permission to *begin* attaching `provider` to the account asking.

Connecting is not a sign-in and must never behave like one: without this,
"Connect" would run the ordinary flow and could sign somebody into a
*different* account, or create a third, with nothing on screen to say so.

This half only opens the round trip. The write needs `/auth/oauth/link`
below, which needs a session -- so this ticket travelling in a URL cannot
on its own attach anything to anybody.
Attach the provider account a finished connect round trip identified.

schema.title: Response My Identities Auth Me Identities Get
Response List My Teams Teams Get
Response List Team Members Teams  Team Id  Members Get

delete.description: Remove a member, or -- when the ids match -- leave the team yourself.

post.description:
Invite an address to the team, or refresh an existing invitation.

The response carries the link to copy, as it always has. With
`send_email` it is also emailed to the address, after the response.

schema.title: Response List Invites Teams  Team Id  Invites Get

get.description: Unauthenticated on purpose: this is what the link shows a stranger.

schema.title: Response List Projects Teams  Team Id  Projects Get

patch.description:
Rename, re-date, re-lead or move a project through its states.

Setting `archived` retires it from pickers without touching the issues
already in it.

delete.description:
Delete a project. Its issues are kept and left with no project.

Saved views that filtered on it stop filtering on it, and automation rules
conditioned on it are switched off rather than widened to every issue.

schema.title: Response List Labels Teams  Team Id  Labels Get

post.description:
Apply one set of changes to up to 200 of the team's issues.

Transactional: every issue changes or none does. Returns the issues as the
batch left them, in the order they were asked for.

schema.title: Response Bulk Update Issues Teams  Team Id  Issues Bulk Update Post

post.description:
Delete up to 200 of the team's issues, all of them or none.

A POST rather than a DELETE with a body, which too many clients and
proxies drop. Each issue goes the way a single delete takes it --
attachments with it, sub-issues promoted.

get.description:
Story-point rollups by column and by assignee for the whole team.

Separate from the issue list because the list is paginated: summing a page
would silently report the total of whatever the client happened to load.

post.description:
Place a card between two others on the board, optionally in another
column. Its neighbours are named, never its new position's key -- the
server works that out, so a client never has to.

get.description:
What has happened to an issue: status, priority, assignee, estimate,
cycle and project changes, oldest first, with who made each one.

The latest 100 changes. The values an issue was created with are its
starting point rather than changes, and are left out.

schema.title: Response List Issue Events Issues  Issue Id  Events Get

delete.description:
Delete an issue and everything that only existed because of it.

Attachments go with it, bytes included -- see
`lib_softtrack/issues.py`. Sub-issues do not: they are promoted to top
level rather than destroyed.

get.description:
Every relationship this issue has, grouped by how it reads from here.

A `blocks` row appears under `blocks` for the source issue and under
`blocked_by` for the target -- one stored row, two readings.
What moving the issue to `team_id` would change, without changing it.

post.description:
Move the issue, and its sub-issues, to another team (#98).

It takes the target team's next number, and whatever does not exist on the
target team is remapped or cleared -- see `lib_softtrack/transfers.py`.
Needs write access to both teams.

patch.description: Edit your own comment's body. Nobody else's, a team admin's included.

delete.description:
Delete your own comment, or -- as a team admin -- anybody's.

Its attachments are deleted with it.

put.description:
React to a comment. Idempotent: reacting twice is reacting once.

Returns the comment's reactions as they now stand, so the client can
redraw the chips without fetching the thread again.

schema.title: Response Add Reaction Comments  Comment Id  Reactions  Emoji  Put

delete.description: Take your own reaction back. Removing one you never gave is a no-op.

schema.title: Response Remove Reaction Comments  Comment Id  Reactions  Emoji  Delete

post.description:
Attach a file to an issue.

The file starts out belonging to the issue. Posting a comment with its id
in `attachment_ids` moves it to that comment -- which is the order the
interface needs, because a screenshot is pasted before the sentence about
it is written.

get.description:
Files attached to the issue itself.

Files belonging to a comment are returned with that comment instead, so
nothing appears twice.

schema.title: Response List Issue Attachments Issues  Issue Id  Attachments Get

get.description: The bytes. Authenticated like every other route, which means an `` cannot fetch it directly -- the browser sends no Authorization header. The frontend loads images through the API client and renders the result as a blob URL. The alternative, a token in the URL, would put a credential into every issue description that embeds an image and into every log line that records the request.

delete.description:
Remove an attachment and its bytes.

Any member of the team may, which matches how the rest of the app treats
issues and comments: membership is the boundary, and there is no
per-object ownership anywhere else to be consistent with.

schema.title: Response List Cycles Teams  Team Id  Cycles Get

post.description: Make this the team's active cycle. Only one may be active at a time.

Close the cycle, carrying unfinished issues into the next one.

Nothing is deleted: if there is no later cycle to carry into, the
unfinished issues go back to the backlog.

get.description:
Points and issues outstanding on each day of the cycle.

Carries the burnup line and the days scope moved, from the same data --
a burndown that hides scope changes makes a team look slow when what
actually happened is that the sprint grew.

A project's scope against its completed work, each day, in issues and points.

Starts on the first day history records anything about the project. Points
only cover sized issues; `unestimated_issues` says how many are not sized,
so the points total is not mistaken for the whole epic.
Committed and completed points for recent completed cycles.
Issue counts per status per day. Widening bands mean work is piling up.
Issues opened against issues closed, with the running backlog.
Time logged during the cycle on issues that were ever in it, by person (#102).
Time logged on the team's issues over the last `days` days, by person (#102).

post.description:
Import a Jira export into this team.

Defaults to a dry run. The dry run takes exactly the same path as the real
one and rolls back at the end, so the report you approve is the report you
then get -- rather than a preview built by separate code that can drift
from what the import actually does.

get.description:
Search issue titles, descriptions and comments.

Always scoped to the teams the caller belongs to. Postgres uses full-text
search with stemming and relevance ranking; SQLite falls back to a
substring match.

parameters.name: team_id

schema.description: Restrict to one team. Defaults to every team you are in.
schema.title: Team Id

parameters.description: Restrict to one team. Defaults to every team you are in.

get.description:
Just the badge. Separate from the list because it is polled and the
list is not -- a poll that dragged fifty rows over the wire to render one
number would be paid for on every open tab.

Every view this person can see on the team, plus which one is default.

Not paginated. A team that has more saved views than fit in one response
has a different problem, and the sidebar renders all of them at once.

put.description:
Where everyone on the team lands. Team admins only, shared views only.

Returns the whole list rather than the view, because setting a default
also unsets the previous one and the sidebar has to redraw both.

Where *you* land on this team, overriding the team's default.

Clearing it falls back to the team's rather than to all issues: no
override means no preference, not a preference for nothing.

get.description: The team's description templates, in picker order. Any member may read.

schema.title: Response List Templates Teams  Team Id  Issue Templates Get

post.description: Add a template. Team admins only.

put.description: Set the picker's order. Takes every template at once.

schema.title: Response Reorder Templates Teams  Team Id  Issue Templates Order Put

get.description: Time spent on the issue: the total, who spent it, and every entry.

post.description: Log time you spent on the issue, on one day.

patch.description: Change one of your own entries.

delete.description: Delete one of your own entries.

get.description:
A server-sent event stream of what changes on the team (#103).

Events are invalidations -- `issue_changed {"id"}`, `comment_added
{"issue_id"}`, `notification {}` for the caller's own inbox, and `resync`
when the stream fell behind -- and never data: the client refetches
through the ordinary endpoints. `close` means the stream is over and must
not be reopened as it was: the caller was signed out, deactivated or
removed from the team. A `: ping` comment every 25 seconds keeps proxies
from dropping it.

Authenticated with the usual bearer header, which is why the browser
reads this with `fetch` rather than `EventSource`: EventSource cannot send
one, and a token in the URL is exactly what this API refuses to do.
The team's board columns, in order. Any member may read them.

schema.title: Response List Statuses Teams  Team Id  Statuses Get

post.description:
Add a column. Team admins only.

Unlike labels and projects, which any member creates: this is the shape of
everybody's board and the vocabulary every report is written in.

put.description:
Set the board order. Takes every status at once -- see StatusOrder.

Declared above `/statuses/{status_id}` so "order" is never read as an id.

schema.title: Response Reorder Statuses Teams  Team Id  Statuses Order Put

delete.description:
Remove a column, moving its issues to another one.

Returns the remaining statuses, because deleting one is the only operation
whose result the board cannot work out for itself -- the issues moved.

schema.title: Response Delete Status Statuses  Status Id  Delete

get.description:
Every rule on the team, enabled or not, in the order they run.

Readable by any member even though only admins may write one: a rule acts
on your issues, so being unable to find out what the rules are is not a
reasonable place to be.

schema.title: Response List Rules Teams  Team Id  Automation Rules Get

post.description: Add a rule. Team admins only, like statuses and unlike labels.

get.description:
What the team's rules have actually done, newest first.

Filterable by rule and by issue, which are the two forms the question
takes: "what has this rule been doing" and "why did this issue move".

delete.description: Remove a rule. Its run log stays -- see automations.delete_rule.

get.description:
The team's connected repositories.

Admins only, unlike the automation rules next to it: this response carries
the webhook secrets, and a secret every member can read is one that has to
be rotated whenever anybody leaves the team.

schema.title: Response List Repositories Teams  Team Id  Repositories Get

post.description:
Connect a repository. Returns the webhook URL and secret to paste into
the provider; nothing happens until the first delivery arrives.

Issue a new secret *and* a new webhook URL -- see the service for why
both move together.

delete.description: Disconnect a repository. Its links come off the issues with it.

get.description:
The branches, commits and pull requests that name this issue.

Any member, unlike the repository list above: this carries no secrets, and
"where is the code for this" is the question the whole feature exists to
answer.

post.description:
A GitHub delivery: `push` and `pull_request` are acted on, the rest
accepted and ignored.

Verified with `X-Hub-Signature-256`, an HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body. The
body has to be read unparsed for that, which is why this route takes a
`Request` rather than a typed model -- FastAPI's parsed body is not the
bytes that were signed.

A GitLab delivery: `Push Hook` and `Merge Request Hook`.

Verified with `X-Gitlab-Token`, which is the secret sent back verbatim
rather than an HMAC. That is weaker than GitHub's scheme -- it is a bearer
secret on the wire, so it depends entirely on TLS -- and it is what GitLab
offers, so it is compared in constant time and left at that.

get.description: The team's outbound webhooks. Team admins only.

schema.title: Response List Webhooks Teams  Team Id  Outbound Webhooks Get

post.description:
Post chosen events to a URL, signed with `X-SoftTrack-Signature`.

The URL must be public unless WEBHOOK_ALLOW_PRIVATE_TARGETS is set. The
reply carries the signing secret -- the only time it is shown.

get.description: The latest deliveries, newest first, with the receiver's answer.

schema.title: Response List Deliveries Outbound Webhooks  Webhook Id  Deliveries Get

post.description: Queue a `ping` delivery, to check the URL and the secret.

AdminUserRead.title: AdminUserRead
AdminUserRead.description: A row in the site admin's user directory.

ApiTokenCreated.title: ApiTokenCreated
ApiTokenCreated.description: Returned once, when the token is made. The only time the secret is seen.

AssigneeLoad.title: AssigneeLoad
AssigneeLoad.description: What one person is carrying. `user` is null for unassigned work.

AttachmentPreview.title: AttachmentPreview
AttachmentPreview.description: How a file can be shown without downloading it (#101).

AuthConfig.title: AuthConfig
AuthConfig.description: What the sign-in pages need to know before anyone has authenticated.

AutomationRuleUpdate.title: AutomationRuleUpdate
AutomationRuleUpdate.description:
Every field optional: renaming a rule, rewriting it and switching it
off are separate gestures and each sends only what it changed.

The trigger can be changed. It reads like a different rule afterwards, but
refusing would only mean people deleting and recreating -- and losing the
run log's link to the rule in the process.

AutomationRunRead.title: AutomationRunRead
AutomationRunRead.description:
One line of the run log.

Carries the rule's name rather than only its id, and `rule_id` is null
once the rule is gone -- the log outlives it on purpose. See
AutomationRun.

AutomationTrigger.title: AutomationTrigger
AutomationTrigger.description:
What makes an automation rule look at an issue.

Eight, and not extensible by a team. Every one of them is something
SoftTrack already writes down as it happens, which is what keeps the
engine to "read the event, read the rules, apply them" instead of a
scheduler with a clock of its own. There is deliberately no "every
Monday": a rule that fires while nobody is doing anything is a rule
nobody remembers exists when it surprises them.

The last three arrive from a connected repository rather than from
somebody using the tracker. They are triggers rather than a settings pair
of their own -- "which status means in review", "which means shipped" --
because that pair is a second engine for "when X happens, change the
issue", and this one already exists, already has conditions, and already
writes down what it did.

file.title: File
file.description: A Jira CSV or JSON export.

dry_run.title: Dry Run
dry_run.description: Report what would happen without writing anything.

CodeLinkKind.title: CodeLinkKind
CodeLinkKind.description: What kind of thing in a repository is linked to an issue.

CodeLinks.title: CodeLinks
CodeLinks.description:
Everything connected to one issue, in the three groups it reads as.

Grouped in the response rather than sorted in the browser, the same way
IssueLinks is: the three have different shapes on the page -- a pull
request has a state, a commit has a sha -- so a flat list would be
regrouped by every client that rendered it.

CommentUpdate.title: CommentUpdate
CommentUpdate.description:
A new body for a comment (#93). The body is the only thing that changes:
its files stay as they were posted, and removing one is done on the file.

ConnectedIdentity.title: ConnectedIdentity
ConnectedIdentity.description:
One provider account that can sign in as the current user.

Only ever returned for yourself. Which third parties hold a key to an
account is the account holder's business, and listing somebody else's
would say which services they use.

CycleCompletion.title: CycleCompletion
CycleCompletion.description: The result of completing a cycle.

CycleProgress.title: CycleProgress
CycleProgress.description:
How much of the cycle's work is done.

Issues and points are reported separately because they disagree, and the
disagreement is the interesting part: eight of ten issues done with two
points of thirty burned means the hard work is all still ahead.

CycleState.title: CycleState
CycleState.description:
Where a cycle is in its life.

Derived from dates would be simpler, but a team that forgets to start a
cycle on Monday should not have Monday counted against its burndown, and a
cycle that runs a day long should not silently complete itself and carry
work away. So the state is set deliberately and the dates are the plan.

DefaultViewUpdate.title: DefaultViewUpdate
DefaultViewUpdate.description: Null clears the default rather than setting one.

DueFilter.title: DueFilter
DueFilter.description:
The due-date questions the board can be narrowed to (#87).

Three questions rather than a date range: they are what a standup asks,
and "this week" means the viewer's week -- the client sends its own
today, so a filter saved on a Sunday evening in Sydney does not quietly
mean London's Sunday.

ImportReport.title: ImportReport
ImportReport.description:
What an import did, or would do.

The same shape for a dry run and a real one, so what you approve is
literally what you then get.

InvitePreview.title: InvitePreview
InvitePreview.description:
What the invite link shows to someone who is not signed in yet.

Deliberately thin. Anyone holding the link can read it, so it says enough
to decide whether to accept -- which team, from whom, as what -- and
nothing about the team's contents or its other members.

InviteRead.title: InviteRead
InviteRead.description:
A pending invitation, as an admin of the team (or its recipient) sees it.

Carries the token so the link can be copied out of this response and sent
by whatever the team already uses -- which works on every instance, with
or without a mail server. Only ever returned to a team admin or to the
person the invite is addressed to.

IssueBulkChanges.title: IssueBulkChanges
IssueBulkChanges.description:
What to do to every issue in the batch. Omitted fields are left alone.

The same unset-versus-null distinction as `IssueUpdate`: an explicit null
assignee, project or cycle clears it on every issue.

issue_ids.title: Issue Ids
issue_ids.description: Between 1 and 200 issues, all on this team.

issue_ids.title: Issue Ids
issue_ids.description: Between 1 and 200 issues, all on this team.

estimate.title: Estimate
estimate.description: Story points on the scale 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. Null means not sized yet, which is distinct from an estimate of zero.

IssueEventField.title: IssueEventField
IssueEventField.description: Which field an IssueEvent records a change to.

IssueEventRead.title: IssueEventRead
IssueEventRead.description:
One change to one field of an issue, as the Activity feed shows it (#81).

`old_value`/`new_value` are what the history stores: a status *category*
(see `_status_category` in history.py), a priority, an estimate, or a
row id. For the id fields -- assignee, cycle, project -- the labels carry
the name it has now, or null when that row has since been deleted.

IssueGrouping.title: IssueGrouping
IssueGrouping.description:
What the board's columns, and the list's sections, are made of.

A saved view stores one (#63), so "the planning view" can open grouped by
project while "my bugs" opens by status. Status is the default because it
is what the board always was.

IssueLinkType.title: IssueLinkType
IssueLinkType.description:
How one issue relates to another.

Only three are stored. "Blocked by" and "duplicated by" are not types --
they are the same rows read from the other end, which is what keeps the
two issues from ever disagreeing about their relationship.

`relates_to` is symmetric, so it is stored once and shown identically on
both issues.

IssueMove.title: IssueMove
IssueMove.description:
Where a card was dropped on the board (#88).

The cards it landed between, as the board showed them: `above_id` is the
one now above it, `below_id` the one below. Either is null at the top or
bottom of a column, and both are null in an empty one. `status_id` moves
it to another column at the same time.

IssueSort.title: IssueSort
IssueSort.description: What the issue list can be ordered by (#88).

IssueTemplateOrder.title: IssueTemplateOrder
IssueTemplateOrder.description:
Every template on the team, in the order the picker should list them.

All of them at once, like `StatusOrder` and for the same reason: two admins
dragging would otherwise interleave into an order neither chose.

IssueTime.title: IssueTime
IssueTime.description: Everything the issue panel shows about time spent on one issue.

IssueType.title: IssueType
IssueType.description:
What kind of work an issue is (#89).

A fixed three, deliberately: per-team custom types are how Jira's type
list grew until nobody could say what a "Sub-task (Technical)" was.

There is no `epic`. An epic is a Project (#60-#64) -- a grouping of issues
with a lead, a target date and progress -- and making it a type as well
would give the tracker two competing ways to say "these belong together".

estimate.title: Estimate
estimate.description: Story points on the scale 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. Null means not sized yet, which is distinct from an estimate of zero.

LinkedIssue.title: LinkedIssue
LinkedIssue.description: Just enough of the other issue to render a row and click through.

NotificationIssue.title: NotificationIssue
NotificationIssue.description:
Enough of the issue to render the row and navigate to it.

`team_key` and `number` rather than a URL: the inbox links into the app's
own routes (`/:teamKey/issue/:issueNumber`), and a server-built path would
be a second place that has to change when they do.

NotificationKind.title: NotificationKind
NotificationKind.description:
Why a notification was raised.

Deliberately about *what happened*, not about how the recipient came to
care -- "someone commented" reads the same whether you are watching the
issue because you filed it or because you were assigned it. Which of
those is true is not information the inbox has any use for.

NotificationUpdate.title: NotificationUpdate
NotificationUpdate.description: Marking one notification read, or putting it back.

OAuthExchange.title: OAuthExchange
OAuthExchange.description:
Redeeming a finished sign-in for a session.

Two halves that travelled separately: the ticket came back in a URL
fragment, and the handshake never left the tab that started the sign-in.
Either one alone is worth nothing, which is what stops a link somebody was
sent from signing them into the sender's account.

OAuthLink.title: OAuthLink
OAuthLink.description:
Finishing a connect: the result the callback handed back.

Spent with a bearer token for the same account, which is what keeps the
ticket that opened the round trip from being a credential of its own.

OAuthLinkTicket.title: OAuthLinkTicket
OAuthLinkTicket.description: Permission for one signed-in person to *begin* attaching one provider.

OAuthLinked.title: OAuthLinked
OAuthLinked.description: Which provider was just attached, so the page can say so.

OAuthProvider.title: OAuthProvider
OAuthProvider.description:
An identity provider somebody can sign in with.

Two, and closed on purpose. Each one is a different set of quirks rather
than a row of configuration -- see `lib_identity/oauth_providers.py` -- and
a self-hosted instance that configures neither keeps email and password
with no external dependency at all. Unrelated to `GitProvider`: that is a
repository SoftTrack is told about, this is a way into an account.

OutboundWebhookCreated.title: OutboundWebhookCreated
OutboundWebhookCreated.description: Returned once, when the webhook is made: the only time the secret is seen.

ParentRef.title: ParentRef
ParentRef.description: Just enough of the parent to render a breadcrumb.

ParsedIssue.title: ParsedIssue
ParsedIssue.description: One issue as read out of an export, before anything is written.

ProjectBurnupPoint.title: ProjectBurnupPoint
ProjectBurnupPoint.description: What one project -- an epic -- held at the end of one day (#64).

ProjectState.title: ProjectState
ProjectState.description:
Where a project -- which is what SoftTrack calls an epic -- is in its life.

Set by hand, like CycleState and for the same reason: "every issue is
done" is evidence a project is finished, not a decision that it is. A
project can be complete with a stray follow-up still open, or have every
issue closed and still be waiting on a launch.

ProjectUpdate.title: ProjectUpdate
ProjectUpdate.description:
Every field optional: renaming, retiring and re-dating are separate
gestures and each sends only what it changed. Send `lead_id` or
`target_date` as null to clear it.

PullRequestState.title: PullRequestState
PullRequestState.description:
Where a pull request is. Only meaningful for `CodeLinkKind.pull_request`.

`merged` and `closed` are separate states rather than one "not open",
because the whole point of the distinction is that one of them shipped
the work and the other did not.

ReactionEmoji.title: ReactionEmoji
ReactionEmoji.description:
The reactions a comment can get (#96) -- GitHub's eight, and only those.

A fixed set rather than any emoji: no picker to build, no emoji data to
ship, and a count that means the same thing on every comment. Stored by
name rather than as the character, so the value is plain ASCII in every
database and every client, and the glyph is the frontend's business.

ReactionSummary.title: ReactionSummary
ReactionSummary.description:
One emoji on one comment, and who gave it (#96).

Summarised rather than one row per reaction: a chip needs the count, the
names for its tooltip, and whether it is yours to take back -- never the
individual rows.

RepositoryLinkedItem.title: RepositoryLinkedItem
RepositoryLinkedItem.description: Which repository a link came from, for an issue that has several.

RepositoryRead.title: RepositoryRead
RepositoryRead.description:
A connected repository, as the settings page receives it.

Carries the secret. There is no point hiding it: the person reading this
page is a team admin, it has to be pasted into the provider's settings
form, and a "shown once" secret only means the rotate button gets used as
a "show it again" button. What it does mean is that this response is
admin-only -- see the router.

ResetPassword.title: ResetPassword
ResetPassword.description: The token from a reset link, and the password to set with it.

RuleActions.title: RuleActions
RuleActions.description:
What a rule does to an issue it matched.

Every field is optional and this model asserts nothing about the
combination, because it is also the shape a *stored* rule is read back in
-- and a stored rule can be left with no actions at all. Deleting a cycle
strips `set_cycle_id` out of the rules that filled it and switches them
off, and a rule in that state has to survive being listed so that somebody
can see it and decide what it should say instead.

The two things a rule being *written* may not do -- nothing at all, and
naming both a cycle and the active one -- are checked on
AutomationRuleCreate and AutomationRuleUpdate, which is where writing
happens.

RuleConditions.title: RuleConditions
RuleConditions.description:
Which issues a rule acts on, out of the ones its trigger reaches.

Nested rather than flattened into the rule models so that "what a rule
matches" is one shape wherever it appears -- the same reason ViewFilters
is nested, and near enough the same vocabulary. Null everywhere means
"every issue this trigger sees", which is what an unconditioned rule
should do rather than one that matches nothing.

SavedViewUpdate.title: SavedViewUpdate
SavedViewUpdate.description:
Every field optional: renaming, re-filtering and sharing are separate
gestures in the UI and each sends only what it changed.

SavedViews.title: SavedViews
SavedViews.description:
The whole sidebar in one response.

The defaults come back with the list rather than from their own endpoint
because the sidebar cannot render a row without knowing whether it is
starred, and a second request would mean a frame where none of them are.

StatusCategory.title: StatusCategory
StatusCategory.description:
What a status *means*, as opposed to what a team calls it.

Fixed on purpose, and the reason per-team statuses are safe to allow at
all. Everything that has to reason about work -- burndown, velocity, "is
this cycle finished", "3 of 5 sub-issues done", whether a blocker still
blocks -- asks the category, never the name. A team can add "Blocked" or
"QA" without any of that having an opinion about it.

Unconstrained workflow states are how Jira became Jira. These five are the
line.

StatusDelete.title: StatusDelete
StatusDelete.description:
Where the issues in the status being deleted should go.

Required rather than defaulted. Issues are the point of the tracker, and
guessing which column somebody's work should land in is not a decision to
make on their behalf.

StatusLoad.title: StatusLoad
StatusLoad.description: The work sitting in one board column.

StatusOrder.title: StatusOrder
StatusOrder.description:
The team's statuses, in the order the board should show them.

Every id at once rather than one move at a time: two people dragging
columns would otherwise interleave into an order neither of them chose.

StatusRead.title: StatusRead
StatusRead.description:
A team's status, as everything that renders an issue receives it.

Embedded in IssueRead rather than referenced by id: a search hit and a
linked issue are both drawn outside any team's board, where there is no
status list on hand to look the id up in.

TeamRole.title: TeamRole
TeamRole.description:
What someone may do inside one team.

Ordered from most to least power. `guest` (#104) sees everything a member
sees -- board, list, issues, comments, cycles, reports, search -- and
changes nothing: no issues, no comments, no settings. The one thing a guest
does write is their own relationship to the team: watching an issue,
choosing their own default view, and leaving.

TeamUpdate.title: TeamUpdate
TeamUpdate.description:
What an admin may change about a team.

No `key`: identifiers like ENG-42 are already in commit messages, chat
logs and browser history, and renaming the prefix would strand every one
of them. See README.

TimeSpent.title: TimeSpent
TimeSpent.description: A rollup for a report: how much time, and whose (#102).

TransferPlan.title: TransferPlan
TransferPlan.description:
What moving an issue to another team would change, before it does.

The confirmation dialog shows this, and `transfer_issue` carries out the
same plan -- they are computed by one function, so the summary a person
agreed to is the change they get.

UnreadCount.title: UnreadCount
UnreadCount.description: The badge. Its own endpoint because it is polled, and the inbox is not.

UserMatch.title: UserMatch
UserMatch.description: A person named in the export, and who they were matched to.

UserMe.title: UserMe
UserMe.description:
The signed-in user's own record.

A superset of UserPublic rather than a separate model: what the account
can do instance-wide is the user's business, and nobody else's, so it is
only ever returned for `me`.

ViewFilters.title: ViewFilters
ViewFilters.description:
What a view narrows the issue list to.

Nested rather than flattened into the view models so that the same shape
is what the board sends, what a view stores, and what the frontend keeps
in the URL -- one type to keep in step instead of three.

Null everywhere means "all issues", which is what an empty view is.

WebhookEvent.title: WebhookEvent
WebhookEvent.description:
What an outbound webhook can be sent (#91).

The same happenings the notification system already observes, named the
way most senders name theirs: `resource.verb`.

WebhookReceipt.title: WebhookReceipt
WebhookReceipt.description:
What the webhook endpoint answers with.

More than an empty 200 on purpose. Both providers show the response body
in their delivery log, and that log is the entire debugging surface for
whoever is setting this up -- "accepted, matched nothing" is the answer to
the question they are about to ask, and it is much cheaper to read there
than to work out from an issue page that did not change.

ErrorCode.description: Every code the API can return. Grouped by what the client did wrong.
ErrorCode.title: ErrorCode

ApiErrorBody.description: The body of every error raised with a code.
ApiErrorBody.title: ApiErrorBody
